birthplace: Clifton, then in Gloucestershire and now part of Bristol, son of Dr Thomas Beddoes the physician and chemist and of Anna Maria Beddoes (née Edgeworth), sister of Maria Edgeworth
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the morbid and neo-Jacobean wing of British Romanticism, a Catholic-Emigre tradition of unread closet tragedy which took Elizabethan and Jacobean drama as its working model and was formed in the German universities
literary_identity: A physician who wrote plays and poems, and the most considerable English dramatist in the closet between Byron and Swinburne: the author of one early revenge tragedy and of one great tragedy, Death's Jest-Book, which he rebuilt and unbuilt for twenty years and never lived to publish.
biography: Thomas Lovell Beddoes was born at Clifton in the summer of 1803 (30 June is the date now usually given; the eleventh Encyclopaedia Britannica printed 20 July), the son of Dr Thomas Beddoes, physician, chemist and projector of the Pneumatic Institution at Bristol, and of Anna Maria Beddoes, sister of Maria Edgeworth, so that he was bred inside the most argued and most experimental household of late Georgian England. He was educated at Charterhouse and at Pembroke College, Oxford, where he was in residence from about 1820 to 1824, and he began to print while still under age: The Improvisatore appeared in 1821 and The Bride's Tragedy, the revenge drama of his eighteenth year, in 1822. He then took up medicine as his father had done, studying at Göttingen from 1824 and afterwards at Würzburg, where he proceeded to the doctor's degree, and he spent the rest of his life as a practising physician in the German-speaking towns, in poverty, in quarrels with his lodgers, and under the notice of the police for the democratic and republican opinions he vented in verse and prose for German and Swiss periodicals. Behind the medical work went on the unceasing revision of Death's Jest-Book, drafted in the later 1820s, since the text of 1829 survives in manuscript, while The Second Brother, Torrismond and much occasional verse were left in fragment. Illness, debt and disappointment ended in self-destruction: he took poison at Basel on 26 January 1849, usually reported as prussic acid, after surgery on a diseased limb. His friend and executor Thomas Forbes Kelsall printed Death's Jest-Book in 1850 and the posthumous Poems in 1851 with a memoir, and their circulation among the generation of the Pre-Raphaelites secured his survival; Lytton Strachey named him 'the last Elizabethan', H. W. Donner's Oxford edition of the Works of 1935 fixed the canon, and the recovery of the 1829 text of Jest-Book confirmed the estimate of a dramatist who wrote for a theatre he never saw.
literary_profile: His printed work in his lifetime was two thin volumes of narrative and dramatic verse, The Improvisatore (1821) and The Bride's Tragedy (1822); almost everything else appeared after his death, above all the five-act Death's Jest-Book, privately printed in 1850, and the posthumous Poems of 1851, which gather The Second Brother, Torrismond, dramatic scenes and fragments, miscellaneous lyrics, sonnets and versions from the Greek anthology. He is therefore a dramatist first and a lyric poet second: two completed plays in verse, a body of short reflective and occasional lyrics, and a critical and polemical margin of German journalism, of scholarship on Greek tragedy and of correspondence, none of which he reduced himself into a book.
stylistic_characteristics: A deliberate archaism of diction and syntax learnt from the Jacobeans: compounds, reduplications and obsessions of phrase, an anatomical and clinical vocabulary turned to metaphor, and imagery of corpses, drugs, dissection and sleep. His verse moves in long, musical, heavily alliterating lines broken by asides and stage business, and his later drama interplots comedy, philosophy and ghostcraft so fiercely that plot is sacrificed to verbal and intellectual energy. The lyrics are more controlled than the plays, and the whole work is marked by a self-quoting, revisionary habit of mind, since he reworked the same scenes and the same images for two decades.
intellectual_concerns: Death as an object of knowledge rather than of piety; the identity of the person across dissolution and resurrection; the credibility of ghosts, dreams and the post-mortem senses; suicide and the will to die, considered with a physician's exactness and a dramatist's self-interest; the ethics of experiment on living bodies, in his father's line; Greek tragedy, its machinery and its civic religion; and republican liberty, which he attached to his medical practice and paid for with his livelihood.
historical_significance: He carries on into the nineteenth century the old English tragedy of revenge and of the grave, and makes it the vehicle of a specifically modern morbidity; through the 1850 volumes he passed into the inheritance of the Pre-Raphaelites, of the decadent poets and of the twentieth-century revivals of verse drama, and he is the standing example of the 'closet drama' that is unread because unperformable. His case is also a document of Romantic medical culture, of the intellectual exile of a British radical in the German states, and of the transmission of Coleridgean and Wedgwood-Edgeworth family networks into a generation that knew its own inheritance as a debt.
biographical_uncertainty: His birth is unsettled and the older catalogues and this project's list of installments give 1813 and Cannon Street, London, whereas modern authorities give 30 June 1803 at Clifton, with the 1911 Encyclopaedia printing 20 July; his birthplace has also been reported as Clifton in Shropshire; the place of his death is variously given as Basel and as Frankfort-on-the-Main, and the poison as prussic acid or as curare, and the dating of his drafts of Death's Jest-Book and the extent of Kelsall's editorial reconstruction remain matters of argument.

birthplace: On the Bristol side of the Severn at Kingsdown, Gloucestershire, according to modern authorities, though the Dictionary of National Biography gave Clevedon, Somerset; eldest child of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Sara Fricker Coleridge
nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; the Lakeland and Wordsworth-Coleridge circle of British Romanticism inherited by the second generation, and the province of the magazine essay, of old-dramatist scholarship and of northern biographical compilation
literary_identity: A poet of sonnets and short occasional lyrics, an essayist and biographer of the early English dramatists, and a schoolmaster who never held a steady post; the most celebrated instance in English letters of brilliant promise unfulfilled, and by inheritance and by friendship the closest surviving link between Wordsworth, his father and the Victorian man of letters.
biography: Hartley Coleridge was born on 19 September 1796, the eldest child of Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Sara Fricker Coleridge, and was named after David Hartley, the associationist philosopher of his father's early allegiance; he is the infant addressed in 'Frost at Midnight'. His childhood was passed mainly in the Lake District, where he was schooled at Ambleside and, after the Wordsworth family settled at Rydal Mount, enjoyed the unusual privilege of the use of Wordsworth's library; about the age of eight he and his brother Derwent invented the imaginary kingdom of Ejuxria, whose affairs he continued in later years to record and to regret. He went up to Oxford in 1815 and was elected to a fellowship at Oriel College, which he lost within a few years on the ground of intemperance; that loss determined the outline of the rest of his life. Two years in London as a journalistic writer were followed by a return to Ambleside, where an attempt to keep pupils was abandoned about 1830 and he was thrown upon the kindness of friends and of the publisher F. E. Bingley, under whose eye he compiled the Biographia Borealis of 1833 and printed the small volume of Poems of the same year. The Worthies of Yorkshire and Lancashire followed in 1836, and his scholarly work on the old drama issued in the memoirs and editing of Massinger and Ford of the late 1830s and about 1840, while he wrote at intervals for Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine and the London Magazine and in 1837 and 1838 helped to manage Sedbergh grammar school. Dependency on alcohol, embarrassment of money and a constitutional indolence defeated every plan of steady work; he died of bronchitis on 6 January 1849 and was buried in Grasmere churchyard within sight of Wordsworth's grave. His brother Derwent Coleridge edited his Poems and his Essays and Marginalia, four volumes in all, in 1851, and his letters, an indispensable record of the Coleridgean household, were edited in the twentieth century, as modern reassessment has established the sonnets and the dramatic criticism as a considerable minor body of work.
literary_profile: His verse is small in bulk and almost all occasional: the Poems of 1833, enlarged in the two volumes of 1851, consist of sonnets on friendship, on the Lakeland landscape, on books and on his own defeat, together with ballad-measure pieces, translations and fragments such as the Prometheus; the longer narrative and dramatic projects remained unfinished. His prose divides between biographical compilation, in the Biographia Borealis of 1833 and the Worthies of Yorkshire and Lancashire of 1836, and dramatic scholarship and criticism, in the memoirs and editing of Massinger and Ford and in the magazine essays which the posthumous Essays and Marginalia of 1851 gathered; his correspondence, published as Letters, is a third and perhaps the most valuable part of his work.
stylistic_characteristics: A compressed, plain and deliberately unimpassioned manner of verse, in which the sonnet of ten or twelve lines carries the argument in a single sentence of argument and close with a sententious turn; a fondness for the abstract noun, for balance and antithesis, and for the colloquial idiom of cultivated speech, with an occasional Jonsonian point and an occasional Wordsworthian simplicity of diction. His prose is digressive, allusive and conversational, made of quotations, marginal notes and catalogues of names, and its virtue is rather its range of reading and its good sense than any sustained architecture.
intellectual_concerns: Associationist psychology and the formation of character, inherited from Hartley and argued over with his father; providence, prayer and the morality of a clergyman's family in an age of doubt; the claims of genius against indolence and appetite, and the ethics of self-knowledge; the dignity and the national use of the old English drama; the worthies tradition of regional biography, in which local fame is gathered as evidence of a nation's intellectual history; and the obligations of a son to a father's texts, which made him editor, witness and apologist.
historical_significance: He stands in the history of Romanticism as the living proof of its anxieties of inheritance, the child of the Lyrical Ballads generation whose failure was memorialised by his own father and by Wordsworth and afterwards read as the paradigm of unfulfilled promise. His essays and his edition of the old dramatists kept the Jacobean and Caroline stage before a Victorian public, his northern worthies volumes made regional biography an instrument of literary history, and his letters and conversations are a primary source for the Coleridge family and for Wordsworth at Rydal, giving him a durable, if subordinate, place in the documentation of the period.
biographical_uncertainty: Reference works long antedating the modern calendars give his birth as 1791 and the Dictionary of National Biography gives Clevedon where later scholars give Kingsdown, while the year in which he held and lost the Oriel fellowship is reported variously as about 1819, 1820 and 1826; the long narrative poem 'Davysses', sometimes entered among his works in library catalogues, could not be traced in the printed bibliographies and should be treated as unverified.

birthplace: Kilkenny city, county Kilkenny, on 3 April 1798, son of Michael Banim, a farmer and shopkeeper of the Catholic middle class, and of Judith Banim (née Carroll); Banim is a Kilkenny-Tipperary variant of Bannon, and the brothers were long associated with Callan and with Windgap on the edge of the city
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Catholic Irish tale of peasant life and of the national history which followed Maria Edgeworth and the Waverley model, and which the Banims published as 'the O'Hara Family'. Joint with his elder brother Michael: Tales by the O'Hara Family, first series (1825) and second series (1826), the songs of the Chaunt of the Cholera (1831), The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842). Single-handed: The Celt's Paradise (1821), Damon and Pythias (1821), Revelations of the Dead Alive (1824), The Boyne Water (1826), The Anglo-Irish of the Nineteenth Century (1828) and The Smuggler (1831)
literary_identity: Novelist, tale-writer, dramatist in blank verse, song-writer and essayist, and first an aspirant historical painter; with his brother Michael the founder of the Irish peasant tale written by an Irishman rather than by the Anglo-Irish ascendancy, and long known to English readers as the 'Scott of Ireland'.
biography: John Banim was born in Kilkenny city on 3 April 1798, the son of Michael Banim, a farmer and shopkeeper, and of Judith Carroll his wife, and grew up in the consciously Catholic middle-class world of the Midland townland, where the memory of 1798 and the penal grievance were matter of family fact. He showed early skill with the pencil, studied painting in the Kilkenny and Dublin circle of T. J. Mulvany, and failed to establish himself as a historical painter; his ambition then turned to verse and the stage, and in 1821 he published The Celt's Paradise, a poem in four duans professedly translated from the Irish, and the blank-verse classical tragedy Damon and Pythias, acted at Covent Garden with his friend Richard Lalor Sheil helping on the stage version. Removing to Dublin about 1820 and to London in the early 1820s, he knew poverty and journalism before the success of the first series of Tales by the O'Hara Family in 1825, under the invented name of an Irish family and welcomed for its humour, its landscape and its pathos; the second series of 1826, the anonymous essays of Revelations of the Dead Alive (1824) and the historical novel The Boyne Water (1826), on the settlement of 1690, established him as the chronicler of the Irish tenantry. The Anglo-Irish of the Nineteenth Century (1828), The Denounced (1830) and The Smuggler (1831) followed, and his songs, among them 'Soggarth Aroon', passed into popular recitation. Broken health, failing sight and debt curtailed his later work; The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842), issued jointly with Michael, were his last books, a testimonial was raised for him by his readers, and he died at his cottage at Windgap near Kilkenny in August 1842, aged forty-four. His brother survived him thirty-two years, wrote the notice in The Nation, and helped P. J. Murray with the Life of John Banim of 1857, which fixed his legend as a neglected genius; collected editions kept the O'Hara stories in print through the century, before the twentieth century reduced him to a few anthologised pieces.
literary_profile: He wrote in four genres at once: verse and drama, with The Celt's Paradise (1821) and Damon and Pythias (1821) and a body of Irish song and lyric; the collaborative Irish tale, the two series of Tales by the O'Hara Family (1825, 1826), with 'Crohoore of the Billhook', 'The Fetches', 'John Doe', 'The Nowlans' and 'Peter of the Castle', and the later joint volumes The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842); the single-handed three-volume novel of Irish history and society, The Boyne Water (1826), The Anglo-Irish of the Nineteenth Century (1828), The Denounced (1830) and The Smuggler (1831); and miscellaneous essay and sketch, Revelations of the Dead Alive (1824), reissued in 1845 as London and its Eccentricities in the Year 2023.
stylistic_characteristics: A spoken Hibernian English carried by dialogue, in which the peasant's exuberance, proverb, liturgy and lament are transcribed at length and with evident delight, and the narration breaks into description of place, of weather and of the body's suffering; the comic and the afflictive are placed side by side without transition, and the frame-tale device of the O'Hara family lets a tale tell itself. The blank verse of Damon and Pythias is formal and classical, the songs simple and repetitive, and the essays colloquial, digressive and given to caricature.
intellectual_concerns: The character and the grievance of the Irish poor under the Protestant ascendancy and the penal inheritance; the tenantry, the hedge-school, the priest, the smuggler and the informant as social types; the memory and the judgement of 1798 and of the Williamite revolution; the authenticity of Irish bardic poetry and song; the reading of character by landscape and by weather; the fate of the artist and the man of letters in a country without a market; and the moral economy of debt, drink and patronage.
historical_significance: With his brother he made the Irish peasant tale a distinct branch of the nineteenth-century national tale, Irish in authorship, Catholic in sympathy and realist in observation, and gave the English reading public, which knew Ireland through Edgeworth and through Waverley imitation, its own chronicler; reviewers made him the 'Scott of Ireland' and his vogue prepared the way for Lever, for the fiction of the Nation and for the later Irish revival. His case is also central in the history of collaborative and pseudonymous publication, and his songs and his 'Fetches' ghost tale entered the repertory of Irish popular literature.
biographical_uncertainty: He is called now the eldest and now the younger son of his father, the year of his removal to London is given as 1820 or 1822, the day of his death as 13, 30 or 31 August 1842, and the share of each brother in the O'Hara volumes, in the Chaunt of the Cholera songs and in such tales as 'Crohoore of the Billhook' and 'The Mayor of Windgap', remains disputed in the bibliographies.

birthplace: Kilkenny city, county Kilkenny, on 5 August 1796, elder brother of John Banim and son of Michael Banim, a farmer and shopkeeper, and of Judith Banim (née Carroll)
nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the Catholic Irish tale of the peasantry and of 1798, written in partnership with his brother John under the persona of 'the O'Hara Family'. Joint with John: Tales by the O'Hara Family, first series (1825) and second series (1826), the songs of the Chaunt of the Cholera (1831), The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842). Single-handed, and usually the graver and more historical half of the partnership: The Croppy (1828), The Ghost-Hunter and His Family (1833), The Mayor of Windgap and Canvassing (1835), Clough Fionn (1852) and The Town of the Cascades (1864)
literary_identity: Novelist and tale-writer, the quieter and longer-lived of the two Kilkenny brothers, who carried most of the joint Irish tales after John's fame had begun to fail, added a rebellion novel and a ghost story of his own, and spent his later years as a public servant in his native city and as the custodian of his brother's reputation and papers.
biography: Michael Banim was born in Kilkenny city on 5 August 1796, the elder brother of John Banim, and son of Michael Banim, a farmer and shopkeeper; he was bred in the same Catholic, schoolmaster-ridden, remembrance-obsessed world of Midland Kilkenny that supplied the matter of the O'Hara tales. He was intended for the law, was entered briefly as a student and abandoned it to help in his father's business, and so stayed at home and in Ireland while John tried painting in Dublin and journalism in London. The partnership that made the brothers' name was formed at a distance: he supplied the local knowledge, the Irish speech and much of the substance of the first series of Tales by the O'Hara Family in 1825 and of the second in 1826, and he contributed to the tales afterwards reissued as 'John Doe' and 'The Fetches' while John's share was more widely advertised. After the brothers' quarrels with fortune he published on his own account The Croppy, a tale of 1798, in 1828, the ghost story The Ghost-Hunter and His Family (1833), the country-politics comedy The Mayor of Windgap and Canvassing (1835), and with John the joint volumes The Bit o' Writin' (1838) and Father Connell (1842). On his brother's death in 1842 he became the family's literary executor and its public historian, writing the notice in The Nation and furnishing P. J. Murray with the materials and recollections of the Life of John Banim of 1857. He took a prominent place in the civic and political life of his native city, serving as postmaster of Kilkenny through the 1850s and 1860s and as mayor, and he published late fiction of Irish landscape and tradition, Clough Fionn in 1852 and The Town of the Cascades in 1864. He retired to Booterstown near Dublin, where he died on 30 August 1874, outliving by a generation the fame which had been shared and which the histories of the Irish novel have only lately tried to divide between the brothers again.
literary_profile: His work is narrative and largely Irish in subject: the collaborative peasant and national tale of the two O'Hara series (1825, 1826) and of the later joint books, to which his contributions of local custom, Shrove Tuesday and country-wedding description are considerable; the rebellion novel The Croppy (1828), which made 1798 a matter of sympathy rather of caricature; the supernatural tale The Ghost-Hunter and His Family (1833); the comic country-politics novel The Mayor of Windgap and Canvassing (1835); and the late romances of Irish place and tradition, Clough Fionn (1852) and The Town of the Cascades (1864). He also wrote verse and song with his brother and left memoir and editorial matter on which all later biography of the pair depends.
stylistic_characteristics: A plainly told, oral and dialogic narrative in Irish English, transcribing peasant speech at length, with a strong eye for custom, ceremony and the texture of country business; a heavier and more directly historical seriousness than John's, since the rebellion and the priesthood are handled as public events rather than as picaresque matter; and a fondness for the ghost story's machinery of fetches, warnings and death-beds, where the sentences shorten and the description is repeated for effect. His comedy is of electioneering, of the public house and of the ambitious farmer, and the later prose is more deliberate, more explanatory and more antiquarian.
intellectual_concerns: The justice and the meaning of 1798 and of secret society oathing in Ireland; the priesthood, the Mass-place and the moral order of a penal peasantry; death, haunting and the credibility of the supernatural in a Catholic country; the effect of the union, of electioneering and of the relief and dispensary system upon rural society; the authenticity of Irish names, topography and tradition; the ethics and the economics of joint authorship, and the duty of a brother to a brother's fame.
historical_significance: As the joint author of the Tales by the O'Hara Family he helped to transfer the representation of the Irish peasant from Anglo-Irish management to Irish, Catholic and self-respecting narration, a move that matters in the line running to the fiction of the Nation, to Lever and to the Irish revival; The Croppy is one of the earliest sympathetic Irish novels of the 1798 rebellion, and his ghost and country tales are documents of supernatural and popular-culture writing in the 1830s. He also preserved the record of the partnership, and the uncertainty over which brother wrote what makes him a central instance of the collaborative, pseudonymous production of the early Victorian literary market.
biographical_uncertainty: His birth year is given now as 1796 and now as 1800 in older catalogues, and the elder or younger rank of the brothers is reversed in different sources; attribution between them of the O'Hara tales, of 'Crohoore of the Billhook', 'The Mayor of Windgap' and the Chaunt of the Cholera songs is still disputed, the personae 'Abel' and 'Barnes' O'Hara are assigned inconsistently, and the volume sometimes cited for him as 'The Ghost Book and Other Pictures' could not be traced in the printed bibliographies, which give The Ghost-Hunter and His Family (1833).
